A_rebates_ricardian.orphan: Debt-financed rebates raise household spending without reducing national saving / with no crowding-out cost.
A_rebates_ricardian.q: how governments should design fiscal support for households during a downturn
src: Increases in credit card limits generate an immediate and significant rise in household debt, especially for people near their limit.
Households spent 20 to 40 percent of the 2001 federal tax rebates on nondurable goods within three months of receipt, and about two-thirds within six months.
Government spending multipliers are considerably larger in recessions than in expansions.
Many households hold little liquid wealth despite owning illiquid assets, so about a quarter of fiscal stimulus payments are spent on nondurables within a quarter.
Government budget deficits do not raise real interest rates or depress national saving.
Fiscal consolidation during the euro-area crisis reduced growth more than forecasters expected, implying fiscal multipliers were larger than assumed.

C_monetary_timing.orphan: Predictable, well-communicated (anticipated) policy maximizes real effects, while effects also depend on wage-contract timing; or: lower policy volatility makes systematic policy more powerful.
C_monetary_timing.q: how a central bank should time and communicate policy changes to make them as effective as possible
src: The output response to a monetary policy shock depends on when in the year it occurs, because wage contracts are staggered unevenly across quarters.
Firms with stickier prices show larger stock-return volatility after monetary policy announcements, indicating that costs of changing prices matter.
Monetary policy shocks have medium-sized real effects on output.
Across 47 countries, the short-run effect of monetary shocks on real output is smaller where monetary shocks are more variable.
Deliberate anti-inflationary shifts in Federal Reserve policy raised unemployment by about two percentage points, with persistent effects.
Once information effects are accounted for, monetary tightening is unequivocally contractionary for demand, labor and credit markets.

D_multiplier_regime_control.q: how large fiscal multipliers are and when governments should use spending stimulus
src: Government spending multipliers are considerably larger in recessions than in expansions.
At the zero lower bound with excess capacity, expansionary fiscal policy is likely to be self-financing.
Consumption is insensitive to whether government spending is financed by taxes or debt, and government spending partly substitutes for private consumption.
Across 98 studies, spending multipliers are about 0.7 to 0.9 higher during downturns and exceed one for most spending categories.
Fiscal multipliers are overwhelmingly positive but small, and fiscal contractions can sometimes be expansionary.
In G7 economies, spending and revenue multipliers tend to be larger in downturns than in expansions.

E_same_framework_control.q: how labor-market frictions shape the costs of recessions and the role of monetary policy
src: Downward nominal wage rigidity under a currency peg causes involuntary unemployment in contractions; capital controls can reduce it by about 5 percentage points.
Downward nominal wage rigidities shape the slope and curvature of the Phillips curve and recent U.S. unemployment dynamics.
Nominal wages in Indian village labor markets rise in good times but do not fall in droughts, and this ratcheting reduces employment by about 9 percent.
An estimated macro model with staggered nominal wage bargaining fits U.S. data better than a flexible-wage version.
The output response to a monetary policy shock depends on when in the year it occurs, because wage contracts are staggered unevenly across quarters.
With real-wage rigidities and staggered prices, unemployment fluctuations are inefficient and the central bank faces a trade-off between stabilizing inflation and unemployment.
